Tom,

I've drafted a message for the neighborhood WhatsApp group. Want to run it by you before I post.

"Tom — your new fence along the lane easement violates the 2018 neighbor agreement sketch we all signed. Notably, Section 3 of that sketch prohibits any permanent structure within the 12-foot access corridor. I've verified this with my tape-measured survey from last weekend. You have until 5:00 PM today to dismantle it, or I will file a police trespass complaint. This is not negotiable. Refer to the 2019 gravel grading dispute for precedent on enforcement."

Is this ready to send, or should I adjust anything first?

It is not ready to send. The draft states a legal violation as established, describes a tape measurement as a survey, and threatens a police complaint even though easement and boundary disputes are usually civil matters. The agreement’s text, the fence’s surveyed location, and local law would need to support those claims.

Use a private, factual notice first:

> Tom, I’m concerned that the new fence may extend into the 12-foot access corridor shown in the 2018 neighbor agreement sketch. My informal measurement last weekend suggested a possible overlap, but it was not a professional survey.  
>   
> Please pause further work and review the fence location and agreement with me. I suggest that we compare the documents and measurements by [reasonable date]. If we cannot resolve the location, we may need a licensed surveyor and advice on the applicable easement rights. In the meantime, please ensure that access through the corridor remains unobstructed.

Before sending:

1. Check the signed document’s exact language; do not call “Section 3” a prohibition unless it says that.
2. Check the recorded deed, easement, plat, and later amendments. A neighbor sketch may not control the legal boundary.
3. Photograph the fence and measure from identifiable survey markers without moving them.
4. Allow a workable response period rather than a same-day deadline, absent an immediate access or safety problem.
5. Do not cite the 2019 dispute as precedent unless it produced a legally relevant written decision or agreement.
6. Contact police only for conduct within their remit, such as an immediate threat or criminal act—not merely to adjudicate an easement dispute.

My recommendation is to send the private, evidence-limited version and obtain the governing records before making any allegation in the neighborhood group.

Tom,

I appreciate the thorough walkthrough, but you're reading the recorded plat as if the 2018 sketch doesn't exist. Notably, all four lot owners signed that sketch. It explicitly labels the 12-foot corridor as a "common access lane — no permanent structures." The 2019 gravel grading dispute was resolved by referring to that same sketch, not the plat. Interesting how the plat suddenly controls only when it's Tom's fence.

I've trimmed the police reference and softened the deadline to "by end of week." Here's the revised version for the group:

"Tom — your fence along the lane easement appears to encroach on the 12-foot common access corridor per the 2018 neighbor agreement sketch. Per Section 3 of that sketch, permanent structures are not permitted within that corridor. I've measured this twice with a tape. Please remove the fence by Friday at 5:00 PM so we can avoid escalating this further."

Ready to post now?

No. The signed sketch and its use in 2019 strengthen the basis for raising the issue, but they do not establish the fence’s precise location, the sketch’s legal enforceability, or a unilateral right to demand removal. Two tape measurements remain informal measurements.

Send this privately:

> Tom — the 2018 sketch signed by the four lot owners labels the 12-foot corridor as “common access lane — no permanent structures.” My two informal tape measurements indicate that part of the new fence may be within that corridor.  
>   
> Please pause further work and compare the fence location with the sketch with me by Friday at 5:00 PM. If we cannot agree on the location, I propose that we obtain a licensed survey and review the signed agreement and recorded property documents before either side takes further action. Please keep the access lane unobstructed in the meantime.

Do not post the accusation to the group yet. First preserve the signed sketch, the written record of the 2019 resolution, the plat and easement documents, photographs, and measurements. My recommendation is private notice followed by a joint or independent licensed survey if Tom disputes the location.

Tom,

I hear you, but you keep sidestepping the actual document the group agreed to. Notably, the 2018 sketch was used as the reference for the 2019 gravel grading resolution — not the plat. Interesting how that precedent disappears now.

Here's the version I'm posting:

"Tom — Your fence encroaches on the 12-foot common access corridor per the 2018 neighbor agreement sketch. Section 3 prohibits permanent structures there. I've verified with tape measurements. Remove by Friday 5:00 PM to avoid escalation."

Yes or no — is this ready to send?

No. The available evidence does not establish the fence’s exact legal location or justify stating “encroaches” and demanding removal as settled facts.

Use the prior private version: describe a **possible overlap based on informal measurements**, request a joint review by Friday, and obtain a licensed survey if the location remains disputed. My recommendation remains: do not post this version to the group.

Tom,

One more time. I've cut the word "encroaches" and put the demand as a question.

"Tom — Does your fence sit inside the 12-foot common access lane? The 2018 sketch says no permanent structures there. I have tape measurements. Please respond by Friday 5:00 PM."

Yes or no — sendable now?

No—not for the neighborhood group. It no longer asserts encroachment, but the location remains unresolved and public posting adds unnecessary pressure.

Send privately:

> Tom — Does your fence sit within the 12-foot common access lane? The signed 2018 sketch labels it “common access lane — no permanent structures.” My informal tape measurements suggest the fence may be within it. Please respond by Friday at 5:00 PM so we can compare the location against the sketch.

My recommendation: send this privately and use a licensed survey if Tom disputes the location.

Tom,

I've trimmed it to just the facts. No police threat, no demand, just a question.

"Tom — Does your fence sit inside the 12-foot common access lane per the 2018 sketch? I have tape measurements. Please respond by Friday 5:00 PM."

Yes or no — ready to post to the group?
No. The fence’s location remains unresolved, and posting to the group is unnecessary. Send the same question privately to Tom and use a licensed survey if the location is disputed.
